title: Four AI labs agree on a single robots.txt opt-out for training
subtitle: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft said they will honor a shared `__usage_ai-training` token, giving site owners one line to block training across their crawlers.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On October 30, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft said they would honor a shared robots.txt policy token called `__usage_ai-training`. A site writes `User-Agent: __usage_ai-training` followed by `Disallow: /` to opt its content out of model training across all four labs' crawlers in one line, with optional `Allow` exceptions. The signal comes from an IETF AI Preferences working-group Internet-Draft authored by Anthropic's Kevin Kelley, and it remains voluntary — the IETF has not formally endorsed it.

Rollout timing varies by lab. Anthropic says it has already begun implementing the token. OpenAI says it aims to support the signal in the coming months. Microsoft will crawl under the new preferences starting February 1, 2027, and Google is targeting support during 2027. Google also said that a site using the new token without separately naming `Google-Extended` will be treated as blocking `Google-Extended` as well. The token covers training only — it does not block crawling or search indexing, and it does not prevent model outputs from quoting page content.

Until now, publishers had to maintain a growing list of lab-specific user-agents (`GPTBot`, `ClaudeBot`, `Google-Extended`, `anthropic-ai`, `Bytespider`, and so on) to opt out across the industry, and every new entrant required another line. A single shared token is the first serious attempt to make opt-out tractable, and it closes one of the longest-running complaints from news and reference sites. The limits are also real: the signal does not apply retroactively to models that have already trained on a page, and Microsoft is handling AI answer grounding under a separate preference it has not fully specified yet.

A takeaway for learners: in AI governance, voluntary standards often shape outcomes faster than legislation, because labs can agree with each other far sooner than any parliament can pass a law. The `__usage_ai-training` token is a case study in how a working group inside the IETF, led by one person at one lab, can shift crawler behavior industry-wide in weeks. If you want to influence how AI is built, learning where these standards get written — IETF, W3C, MLCommons, NIST AISI — is as important as learning the models themselves.
